description: We're a couple of space enthusiasts looking for new experiences and new ways to apply the resources and knowledge that NASA provides.
summary:
Martian Map is an interactive web app, for computer and tablet, in English and Spanish, that works as a survival guide for the first crewed mission to Mars, phase by phase. The crew plans the transfer from Earth, chooses a landing site on a layered map, lives through the transit, explores the site in 3D on real orbital photos, places base hubs, plans driving routes that avoid large craters and steep slopes, and keeps their bodies healthy sol by sol.

It addresses the challenge by layering data from several NASA missions (MGS MOLA topography; MGS TES thermal inertia, dust and albedo; Mars Odyssey THEMIS and Viking imagery; MRO CTX and HiRISE mosaics; Curiosity RAD radiation; and the real Perseverance and Curiosity traverses with their raw images) and crossing it with what the human body needs. Any point on Mars gets a 0–100 score and a clear verdict: viable, marginal or not viable, and why.

It matters because astronaut safety depends on seeing terrain, cold, dust, ice and radiation together, at the scale of a single Marswalk, not just on regional maps. Every figure in the app links to its source: 58 sources, cited inside the app.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Martian Map is an interactive guide to surviving on Mars. It runs in the browser on a computer or a tablet, in English and Spanish, and takes a crew through a mission phase by phase:

1. Plan from Earth. A Hohmann transfer planner computes launch windows, travel time, required delta-v, arrival date and the Martian season (solar longitude, Ls) at arrival. A "See equations and algorithm" dialog walks through every formula step by step, with the numbers of the chosen window. Then the crew picks a landing site on a layered map of Mars with past landing sites, rover traverses, a Martian clock and a report for any point.

2. Transit. The trip day by day, what happens to the body at each stage, a confinement routine, an original minigame and NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight.

3. Descent and on site. A 16 km square of terrain around the landing site (or any place you search), built from MOLA elevation and draped with real orbital photos: the ~6 m CTX mosaics of Jezero and Gale, and the global CTX mosaic elsewhere. You can fly over it, walk or drive in first person with the live conditions at your position, follow the real Perseverance and Curiosity traverses, and open the raw images NASA published at each stop, so the astronaut knows what to expect on arrival. Vehicles: on foot, a pressurized rover (NASA SEV, 10 km/h) and a Perseverance replica (152 m/h), at real speed or a faster exploration speed.

4. Surface. Place habitats, greenhouses, solar plants, ice mines and landing pads; each one gets a viability verdict with the full data breakdown before you place it. Plan driving routes of up to 6 stops that avoid large craters and steep slopes, with distance, time, elevation profile and turn-by-turn guidance.

5. Survival, the heart of the app. A sol-by-sol journal (water, meals, sleep, exercise and accumulated radiation) compared with NASA's numbers, what the body needs each day, and step-by-step guides for emergencies: pressure failure, dust storm, solar radiation event, loss of communication and running out of power.

6. Report. The whole mission in one dashboard, printable or saved as PDF.

HOW IT WORKS

For any point on Mars the app samples seven factors and compares them with what the human body and the base need:

- Water: subsurface ice consistency from SWIM.

- Terrain: MOLA elevation and slope. Large craters from the Robbins and Hynek catalog are the obstacles that driving routes go around.

- Temperature, solar energy, pressure and dust: Mars Climate Database (a climate model).

- Radiation: the dose Curiosity's RAD instrument measured in Gale crater, adjusted by surface pressure (a model based on Guo et al., 2015).

Each hub type weighs these factors differently and returns a 0–100 score and a verdict: viable, marginal or not viable. The phases are linked by data: the arrival date from the Hohmann planner sets the season at landing, and that season changes temperature and dust on the map, in the hubs and in the 3D view. Accumulated radiation is compared with NASA's 600 mSv career limit (NASA-STD-3001).

We are honest about the data: values that come from a model are labeled as modeled in the interface, and where there is no data the app says "no data" instead of showing a zero. The raw NASA and partner products were processed with Python scripts into lightweight grids that the browser loads. Every figure links to its source on the in-app References screen (58 sources). The emergency guides are a general guide written by the team from NASA sources, not an official NASA procedure, and the app says so.

HOW IT ADDRESSES THE CHALLENGE

- A layered, integrated view from several NASA missions: seven kinds of data (optical imagery, thermal infrared, topography, climate, radiation, subsurface ice and craters).

- Astronaut safety first: viability from seven factors, accumulated radiation against NASA's limit, and emergency guides.

- A route that avoids obstacles: driving routes around large craters and steep slopes, with stops along the way.

- Knowing what to expect on arrival: real Perseverance and Curiosity routes and the photos taken at each stop, plus a first-person walk on real orbital photos.

- Format: a tablet application the astronaut can carry (touch targets of at least 44 px, works at 768 px wide), also usable on a computer inside the habitat.

BENEFITS

Mission planners and astronauts see terrain, ice, cold, dust and radiation together for the exact place of a Marswalk, with a clear reason behind every verdict. Students and the public can learn how a crewed mission to Mars is planned, from orbital mechanics to the body's daily needs, with real NASA data and links to every source.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

A starting point for a field tool that a crew could carry on a tablet or see in a helmet display: one place that brings scattered mission data together at the scale of a single excursion. The app is built to grow: each screen is an independent module, so new layers, sites or data sets can be added without rewriting the rest.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

- JavaScript with Vite (no framework), HTML and CSS

- Leaflet (interactive maps with NASA Mars Trek tiles) and three.js (3D terrain and first-person view)

- Python scripts to turn NASA, USGS, PSI and MCD products into the grids the app loads

- Supabase (optional cloud saving of missions and minigame scores)

- Node.js built-in test runner, GitHub and GitHub Actions, hosting on Vercel

- An AI coding assistant (Claude Code), disclosed in the commit history (Co-Authored-By lines) and in the repository's CLAUDE.md

Live app: https://laikaii.vercel.app/

Source code: https://github.com/luispilo119-design/Laika-II
dataRefs: Mars Global Surveyor MOLA, Mission Experiment Gridded Data Record (MEGDR), 16 pixels per degree (NASA PDS Geosciences Node): elevation and slope for the viability score, the 3D terrain and the route elevation profiles.
NASA/JPL Mars Trek WMTS API: basemaps (MOLA color topography, Viking MDIM 2.1, Mars Odyssey THEMIS) and data layers (MGS TES thermal inertia, TES dust cover, TES albedo, MOLA roughness).

MRO CTX and HiRISE imagery through Mars Trek: the ~6 m CTX mosaics of Jezero (Mars 2020 landing system map) and Gale, and the HiRISE orthomosaic of Jezero (produced by USGS Astrogeology for Mars 2020), draped over the 3D terrain.
MRO CTX global mosaic beta01 (NASA/JPL/MSSS data; mosaic by the Caltech Murray Lab, served by Esri): orbital photo for the 3D terrain outside Jezero and Gale.
Perseverance and Curiosity traverses and waypoints (NASA/JPL MMGIS "Where is the rover?" maps): real rover routes on the map and in 3D.
Perseverance and Curiosity traverses and waypoints (NASA/JPL MMGIS "Where is the rover?" maps): real rover routes on the map and in 3D.
Perseverance and Curiosity raw images (NASA/JPL-Caltech; Curiosity also MSSS): the photos taken at each rover stop.
NSSDCA Master Catalog (NASA GSFC): coordinates of the Viking 1 and 2, Pathfinder, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix and InSight landing sites.
Mars Fact Sheet (NASA NSSDCA): gravity, radius and mean molar mass of the atmosphere.
NASA GISS Mars24 Sunclock, algorithm and technical notes: the Martian clock, sol and season (Ls).
NASA-STD-3001 technical briefs OCHMO-TB-020 (radiation protection, 600 mSv career limit) and OCHMO-TB-041 (sleep).
NASA Human Research Program: the 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight and each hazard page, and The Human Body in Space.
Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document, NASA/TP-2015-218570/REV1 (NASA JSC): the crew's daily water, food and other life-support values.
Bussey and Hoffman (2016), Human Mars Landing Site and Impacts on Mars Surface Operations (NASA HQ): distances between the habitat and other hubs.

NASA CHAPEA analog mission, Counteracting Bone and Muscle Loss in Microgravity, Data From NASA Rover's Voyage to Mars Aids Planning (RAD during cruise), Mars Solar Conjunction, Real Martians: protecting astronauts from radiation on Mars, Martian dust storm articles, the InSight retirement article and an ISS emergency drill: survival guides and emergency steps.
Mars 2020: Perseverance Rover mission page, and NASA History "Dawn of the Space Age" (Laika and Sputnik 2, the origin of our team name).
Space Exploration Vehicle (NASA SEV), Perseverance Rover Components and the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle (NSSDCA): vehicle speeds for routes and the 3D view.
projectRefs: ESA (European Space Agency): Mars Climate Database v6.2 (LMD / Open University / IAA / ESA / CNES), a general circulation model that gives temperature, pressure, dust and solar irradiance by place and season. Used for four of the seven viability factors and labeled as modeled in the app.
Subsurface Water Ice Mapping, SWIM4MIM ice consistency maps, 0–1 m and 1–5 m (Planetary Science Institute / NASA): the water factor.
Robbins and Hynek (2012), global database of Mars impact craters of 1 km or larger (USGS Astrogeology): the large craters that driving routes go around.
ESA Mars Express HRSC: part of a blended MOLA + HRSC basemap served by NASA Mars Trek (credited in the app).
Guo et al. (2015), Modeling the variations of dose rate measured by RAD during the first MSL Martian year, The Astrophysical Journal.
Hassler et al. (2014), Mars' surface radiation environment measured with the Mars Science Laboratory's Curiosity rover, Science.
three.js, MIT: 3D terrain and first-person view
upabase JS, MIT: optional cloud saving.
Vite, MIT: development and build tool.
Start screen background: the ASCII black hole was written from scratch for this app; the visual idea comes from BLACK-HOLE by JIN2 (@jin_22ee), credited in the app. No code was reused.
Fonts: Archivo and Space Mono, from Google Fonts (SIL Open Font License).
